d1.task: Write the feature brief for the trial-class request. Fill User story, Fields to collect, Three acceptance checks, One failure state and Most private detail. In your reasoning explain when your success message appears and why a parent should never see it too early. Hands-on completion: Build a small runnable trial-booking prototype alongside your brief. Use a local mock server or in-memory store. Run one successful save and one forced failure; submit the relevant code, actual output and the fix. Success must appear only after the save response. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
d1.question: A parent taps Book, but saving fails. When should the page show “Booking saved”?
options: As soon as the parent taps Book.
Once the request is sent, even without a reply.
Only after the server confirms the booking was saved; show a retry message if saving fails.
When the loading animation stops.
d1.explanation: A tap only starts the request. Wait for the server to confirm the save before showing success.

fields.label: User story
fields.hint: One sentence: a parent wants to request a trial class so they can choose a tutor.
fields.prompt: Who needs the booking page, what do they want, and why?

fields.label: Fields to collect
fields.hint: List only necessary details, such as a name and class time. Give a reason for each.
fields.prompt: Which details must the parent enter?

fields.label: Three acceptance checks
fields.hint: Describe a successful save, missing information, and a time that is already taken. Say what should happen in each.
fields.prompt: What should happen in three test situations?

fields.label: One failure state
fields.hint: Write the message and next step. A failed save must not also show Booking saved.
fields.prompt: What should the parent see when saving fails?

fields.label: Most private detail
options: Parent's phone number
Child's school and class
Preferred slot and time
Parent's full name
fields.hint: Choose one detail below and explain why other parents should not see it.
fields.prompt: Which detail needs the most protection?

d2.task: Review the AI-written booking handler. Name Two trust failures, rewrite it in Corrected handler, write Three negative tests, and pick Where the price comes from. In your reasoning explain why the browser cannot be trusted for these values. Hands-on completion: Run your corrected handler locally with a spoofed user ID, changed price and repeated request. Submit the handler and actual output for all three cases, then fix a failing case. A paper trace or expected output alone does not count. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
d2.question: A booking page sends a user ID and price to the server. Someone changes both before sending. What should the server do?
options: Trust the values because the form checked them.
Accept any price above zero.
Check only that the user ID is a number.
Use the verified sign-in to identify the user and its own records to find the price.
d2.explanation: People can change data sent by a browser. The server must check who is signed in and choose the trusted price.

fields.label: Two trust failures
fields.hint: Explain the fake user ID and changed price, and what harm each could cause.
fields.prompt: What two things could someone change to cheat this booking form?

fields.label: Corrected handler
fields.hint: Use the verified sign-in for identity and the database for price. Use a safe database query.
fields.prompt: What does your fixed server code look like?

fields.label: Three negative tests
fields.hint: Write runnable tests for someone else’s ID, a changed price and the same request twice. Include checks such as expect or assert.
fields.prompt: Which three tests check fake IDs, changed prices and repeat requests?

fields.label: Where the price comes from
options: A slots table on the server, looked up by slot id
A hidden field in the booking form
A value stored in the browser's local storage
The price in the page URL query string
fields.hint: Choose a trusted source. A hidden form field can still be changed.
fields.prompt: Where should the server get the real price?

d3.task: Plan the tutor's booking data. In Tables and columns write the SQL for two or more records. Choose What must never repeat. In Private columns and who sees them, name two fields and who may read them. Explain in your reasoning why your uniqueness rule fits. Hands-on completion: Create the schema in a disposable local SQLite or PostgreSQL database. Insert a valid booking, attempt a duplicate slot and run a privacy-safe query. Submit the SQL and actual results, including the constraint error, then correct a schema issue. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
checks: Give every table a primary key
d3.question: Two parents try to book the same seat at the same time. What reliably prevents a double booking?
options: Hide the Book button after one click.
Ask parents not to book together.
A database rule that allows each class-and-seat pair to be saved only once.
Check the browser’s old list of seats.
d3.explanation: The database must reject the second booking, even when two requests arrive together.

fields.label: Tables and columns
fields.hint: Write SQL instructions to create the tables—lists of stored records—and connect each booking to the right person or class.
fields.prompt: What information goes in each database table?

fields.label: What must never repeat
options: One row per student per batch
One row per seat number in one batch
One row per phone number overall
One row per booking date and time
fields.hint: Add a database rule for a class-and-seat pair that must be unique—saved only once.
fields.prompt: Which booking details must never be saved twice?

fields.label: Private columns and who sees them
fields.hint: Name two private data columns and who may read each: the parent, tutor, or nobody else. Show a query that respects this.
fields.prompt: Which information is private, and who may see it?

link.label: GitHub or demo link (optional)
link.hint: Optional: a diagram or schema file you own (dbdiagram, GitHub). Never share real families' data.

d4.task: Write the Register contract. Give Method and path, a Request body with the inputs, and a Success reply. Choose a Status for already registered and describe Two error replies with when each happens. Explain in your reasoning why you wrote this before asking AI for code. Hands-on completion: Implement a tiny local API matching your contract. Send one valid and two invalid requests using curl or a local client. Submit the handler and actual status/body for each; fix an inconsistent response. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
d4.question: A student registers for a workshop twice with the same email. Which server reply clearly tells the page what happened?
options: Status 409 with an already_registered message.
Status 200 saying a new registration was saved.
No reply until the student gives up.
A different random error each time.
d4.explanation: A 409 status means this request conflicts with an existing record. A clear message lets the page explain that registration already exists.

fields.label: Method and path
fields.hint: Name the HTTP action, such as POST, and the server URL, such as /api/register.
fields.prompt: Which URL and action will the page use to send a registration?

fields.label: Request body
fields.hint: Write the data as JSON, with field names and example values. Use safe made-up details.
fields.prompt: What data will the page send?

fields.label: Success reply
fields.hint: Write a JSON reply with the saved registration reference and a clear result.
fields.prompt: What will the server send back after saving?

fields.label: Status for already registered
options: 409 Conflict
400 Bad Request
422 Unprocessable Entity
200 OK with an error message inside
fields.hint: Choose the status code for a request that conflicts with an existing registration.
fields.prompt: What status number means this student is already registered?

fields.label: Two error replies
fields.hint: Write two different errors with a status number, JSON reply, and the situation that causes each.
fields.prompt: What will the server reply for two different errors?

link.label: GitHub or demo link (optional)
link.hint: Optional: your API notes in a gist, Postman or OpenAPI file you own.

d5.task: Protect the Jaipur pickup form. Choose Where to check stock, then improve the Server validation function from its starter. Add an Error message for a bad phone and an Error message for too many items. In your reasoning explain what the browser should still do. Hands-on completion: Run your validation function locally with a valid order, a bad phone number and too many items. Submit the code and actual outputs, then fix and rerun one missed boundary. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
checks: Say how to fix each mistake
d5.question: A browser allows only 20 items, but someone sends a direct order for 5,000. Only 12 are in stock. What stops it?
options: The browser’s quantity limit alone.
Hiding the order button after the click.
Accepting the order and checking stock tomorrow.
The server checks stock and quantity before saving the order.
d5.explanation: Browser controls can be bypassed. Check the available stock again on the server when the order is saved.

fields.label: Where to check stock
options: In the browser only, for speed
On the server only, at save time
In both, browser for feedback and server as the real guard
Skip it and let the owner fix orders by phone
fields.hint: Choose where the final stock check happens before an order is saved.
fields.prompt: Where should the app check the remaining stock?

fields.label: Server validation function
fields.hint: Check the name, a 10-digit Indian phone number, a known item, and a whole quantity from 1 up to available stock.
fields.prompt: What code checks whether an order is allowed?

fields.label: Error message for a bad phone
fields.hint: Use a helpful sentence that says how to correct the phone number.
fields.prompt: What will you tell someone whose phone number is invalid?

fields.label: Error message for too many items
fields.hint: Explain the available amount and ask the person to reduce the order.
fields.prompt: What will you say when they order more than is available?

link.label: GitHub or demo link (optional)
link.hint: Optional: a repository or gist with your validation code.

d6.question: A page says a booking is confirmed, but no booking is stored. What should you share when asking AI to help?
options: The steps, expected and actual results, and error details, with private data removed.
Real passwords and customer phone numbers.
Only the words “it is broken”.
Every unrelated file without explaining the problem.
d6.explanation: Clear steps and actual results help find the cause. Remove secrets and replace personal details with safe examples.

fields.label: First move
options: Reproduce it myself with one test booking and note exact steps
Ask the AI to rewrite the whole booking page
Restart the server and hope it clears
Check the database tables for old rows only
fields.hint: Choose how you will repeat the problem before changing code.
fields.prompt: What will you do first to find this booking bug?

fields.label: Evidence for the assistant
fields.hint: Include the steps, expected and actual results, and relevant error. Replace secrets and phone numbers with safe examples.
fields.prompt: What real error details can you safely share with AI?

fields.label: Fixed handler
fields.hint: Update the actual code so only the correct success or error message appears after the server replies.
fields.prompt: What does your fixed booking code look like?

link.label: GitHub or demo link (optional)
link.hint: Optional: a link to the issue, commit or pull request where you fixed it.

d7.question: Meera changes a booking number in the address and sees another family’s phone number. What fixes this?
options: Hide the link to the other booking.
The server checks that the booking belongs to Meera or that she has the tutor role.
Check only that Meera has signed in.
Change the colour of the booking number.
d7.explanation: Signing in does not give access to every record. Check permission for the specific booking on the server.

user and admin
parent, tutor and admin
guest, member and owner

200 with an empty booking object
302 redirect to the login page

d8.question: A class has 10 seats and all 10 are taken. Which test catches code that still allows another booking?
options: Test taken = 0 and capacity = 10; expect booking to be allowed.
Check only whether the button has a label.
Test one free seat without testing a full class.
Test taken = 10 and capacity = 10; expect booking to be refused.
d8.explanation: Test the exact limit. When taken equals capacity, the class is full and another booking must be refused.

fields.label: Test to automate first
options: The last-seat boundary (nine of ten taken)
A normal booking with seats free
A booking when the batch is full
An empty-name form submission
fields.hint: Choose an important booking behaviour to protect with an automatic test.

fields.hint: Write runnable tests with inputs and expected results. Include normal, invalid and full-capacity cases.

d9.question: A new website release breaks bookings. The previous code still works with the stored data. What is the safest first recovery?
options: Undo that release, restore the working version, then fix the change separately.
Keep the broken version and wait for complaints.
Delete the booking database.
Make several untested changes directly on the live site.
d9.explanation: Restore the known working version first when it is compatible with the data. Then test the repair before releasing it.

fields.hint: Use a short branch name describing the change, such as fix-booking-message.
fields.prompt: What will you name your separate Git branch?

fields.prompt: What changes will your three small commits save?

fields.label: Rollback plan
fields.hint: Give the safe undo commands and checks. Use only a throwaway local project.
fields.prompt: How will you return to a working version if the change fails?

fields.label: How to merge
options: Squash merge after review, one commit on main
Merge commit, keeping every small commit
Rebase then fast-forward for a straight history
Push straight to main to save time
fields.hint: Choose a merge approach after reviewing and testing the changes. Merging joins the branch into the main version.
fields.prompt: How will you join the checked changes into the main version?

d10.question: Before sharing a booking app, you find a typo, slow loading, and a way to open other families’ private records. What comes first?
options: Fix the typo before checking private records.
Block access to other families’ records and test the fix.
Change the homepage colours.
Ignore the problem because people need to sign in.
d10.explanation: Exposed private records can harm families. Fix and test access checks before treating the app as ready to share.

Confirmation text has a spelling mistake
No alert if bookings stop saving
The page takes three seconds to load on mobile data
